Heart Disease Prediction Using Machine Learning¶

Dataset: heart.csv

This project explores the Heart Disease dataset containing 1,025 records and 13 input features. It includes data preprocessing, Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), and training five classification models: Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, KNN, Naive Bayes, and SVM.

The models are compared using Accuracy, AUC, Precision, Recall, F1-score, and MCC. An interactive Streamlit application is developed to evaluate models and display predictions.

Workflow: Data Loading → EDA → Preprocessing → Model Training → Evaluation → Model Comparison → Streamlit Deployment.

Git Hub Repository link: https://github.com/amanchaudhur/Heart_Disease_ML_Assignment

Streamlit App link: https://ga7v3aub5gxcxdr5mxfsxz.streamlit.app/

16. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) – Conclusion¶

The Exploratory Data Analysis of the Heart Disease dataset provided useful insights into the dataset's quality, distribution and relationships between different features and the target variable.

The following observations were made:

  1. Dataset Overview: The dataset contains 1,025 records and 14 columns, consisting of 13 input features and one binary target variable (target). The average age is approximately 54.63 years, with ages ranging from 29 to 77 years.

  2. Missing Values: No missing values were found in any column. Therefore, the dataset does not require missing-value imputation based on the observed data.

  3. Duplicate Records: The dataset contains 205 exact duplicate rows (20%), leaving 820 unique records. These duplicates require special consideration to prevent data leakage during model training and evaluation.

  4. Target Distribution: The target variable is nearly balanced, with 508 records (49.56%) belonging to class 0 and 517 records (50.44%) belonging to class 1. This balance is beneficial for comparing classification algorithms.

  5. Feature Distributions: The numerical features show different distributions and ranges. Some features, particularly cholesterol (chol) and ST depression (oldpeak), contain relatively high values and potential outliers. Several categorical features are represented using numerical codes.

  6. Correlation Analysis: Chest pain type (cp, +0.456) and maximum heart rate (thalach, +0.424) show notable positive correlations with the target. Exercise-induced angina (exang, −0.447), ST depression (oldpeak, −0.439) and number of major vessels (ca, −0.388) show notable negative correlations. These associations suggest that several features may be useful for classification, although correlation does not establish causation.

  7. Feature Relationships: The boxplots show differences between the target classes, particularly for maximum heart rate and ST depression. However, the distributions overlap, indicating that combining multiple features may be more informative than relying on a single feature.

Final Conclusion¶

Overall, the dataset is suitable for the planned machine learning classification experiments because it contains sufficient records, 13 input features, no missing values and a nearly balanced target variable.

The main data-quality concern is the presence of duplicate records. Therefore, a group-aware train-test split should be used to prevent identical feature records from appearing in both sets. Feature scaling should also be fitted only on the training data to avoid data leakage.

The EDA findings provide a foundation for training and comparing Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gaussian Naive Bayes and Support Vector Machine classifiers using Accuracy, AUC, Precision, Recall, F1-score and Matthews Correlation Coefficient.

17. Train-test splitting and feature scaling¶

We'll use an 80:20 split and group identical feature records to reduce leakage. Scaling and imputation will happen inside each model pipeline, fitted only on training data.

In [20]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

X = df.drop(columns=["target"])
y = df["target"]

groups = pd.util.hash_pandas_object(
    X.reset_index(drop=True), index=False
)

splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(
    n_splits=1,
    test_size=0.20,
    random_state=42
)

train_idx, test_idx = next(splitter.split(X, y, groups))

X_train = X.iloc[train_idx]
X_test = X.iloc[test_idx]
y_train = y.iloc[train_idx]
y_test = y.iloc[test_idx]

print("Training:", X_train.shape)
print("Testing:", X_test.shape)
print("Training class counts:\n", y_train.value_counts())
print("Testing class counts:\n", y_test.value_counts())

assert set(groups.iloc[train_idx]).isdisjoint(
    set(groups.iloc[test_idx])
)

18. Train five classification models¶

In [21]:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.svm import SVC

from sklearn.base import clone

estimators = {
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(
        max_iter=2000, random_state=42
    ),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(
        random_state=42
    ),
    "KNN": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5),
    "Naive Bayes": GaussianNB(),
    "SVM": SVC(
        kernel="rbf",
        probability=True,
        random_state=42
    )
}

models = {}

for name, estimator in estimators.items():
    pipeline = Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
        ("classifier", clone(estimator))
    ])

    pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
    models[name] = pipeline

    print(name, "trained successfully")

Logistic Regression trained successfully
Decision Tree trained successfully
KNN trained successfully
Naive Bayes trained successfully
SVM trained successfully

19. Calculate all six evaluation metrics¶

In [22]:
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    roc_auc_score,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
    f1_score,
    matthews_corrcoef,
    confusion_matrix,
    classification_report
)

results = []

for name, model in models.items():
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

    results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob),
        "Precision": precision_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "Recall": recall_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "F1": f1_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "MCC": matthews_corrcoef(y_test, y_pred)
    })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)
display(results_df.round(4))

17. Model Training, Evaluation and Comparison – Conclusion¶

Five machine learning classification algorithms were successfully trained and evaluated on the Heart Disease dataset: Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Gaussian Naive Bayes and Support Vector Machine (SVM).

The dataset was divided into training and testing sets using a group-aware split to prevent identical feature records from appearing in both sets. The training set contained 821 records, while the testing set contained 204 records. Missing-value imputation and feature scaling were included in the model pipelines.

Model Performance Comparison¶

Model Accuracy AUC Precision Recall F1-score MCC
Logistic Regression 0.8627 0.9434 0.8173 0.9043 0.8586 0.7294
Decision Tree 0.9755 0.9750 0.9785 0.9681 0.9733 0.9507
KNN 0.8971 0.9515 0.9011 0.8723 0.8865 0.7927
Naive Bayes 0.8431 0.9435 0.7981 0.8830 0.8384 0.6901
SVM 0.9265 0.9732 0.9072 0.9362 0.9215 0.8527

Key Observations¶

  1. Decision Tree achieved the best overall performance, with an accuracy of 97.55%, F1-score of 0.9733 and MCC of 0.9507.

  2. SVM was the second-best model, achieving 92.65% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.9215.

  3. KNN achieved 89.71% accuracy, demonstrating reasonably good classification performance.

  4. Logistic Regression achieved 86.27% accuracy, while Gaussian Naive Bayes recorded the lowest accuracy of 84.31%.

  5. The Decision Tree confusion matrix showed 108 true negatives, 91 true positives, 2 false positives and 3 false negatives, resulting in only five incorrect predictions out of 204 test records.

Best Model Selection¶

Based on the evaluation metrics, Decision Tree was selected as the best-performing classification model for this experiment.

It achieved the highest Accuracy, AUC, Precision, Recall, F1-score and MCC among the five models tested. Its high MCC indicates strong agreement between predicted and actual labels on the held-out test dataset.

Final Conclusion¶

The experiment successfully implemented and compared five classification algorithms on the same Heart Disease dataset. All six required evaluation metrics were calculated, and the results demonstrated that the Decision Tree classifier performed best on the selected test partition.

The trained models were saved as .pkl files for integration into the Streamlit application, allowing users to select different models and compare their predictions and evaluation results.

Although the Decision Tree achieved excellent performance, these results are limited to the available dataset and the chosen train-test split. Additional cross-validation and testing on independent data would be necessary to assess generalization and clinical reliability.

Overall, the project demonstrates the complete machine learning workflow, including data preprocessing, exploratory analysis, model training, evaluation, comparison and deployment preparation.
